units.translation: 1569. χεῦμα δι’ ἠπείρου βεβαρημέ〈νοι〉: It is unclear whether he has said "mainland" in the common sense of "land" or "Libya," because the whole inhabited world is divided into three continents: Asia, Europe, Libya. Egypt, according to some, is part of Asia, but according to others, part of Libya.
1571. ἄπωθεν: from a distance. Lᵍ P
1573. διήλυσις: passage through, exit. Lᵍ P
1575. φρίσσουσι: they rise to a height. Lᵍ P
1581. περιρρήδην: instead of "around the circumference." Lᵍ P
1589. εἴσατο: he rushed. Lᵍ Gᵍ Sᵐ P
1599. ἁλοσύδναι: of the sea, from "to sink in the sea" 〈...〉, that is, "to move in the sea."
1608. ὀδακτάζοντι: biting. Lᵍ Sᵐ P
1609. ὁλκήιον Ἀργοῦς: the lower timber of the ship, near the keel, by which the ship is dragged, which is fixed first on the ground when the ship is being built.

1613-16a. αὐτὰρ ὑπαὶ λαγόνων δίκραιρά οἱ: double; for such is the tail of Triton, divided into two. It cut the surface of the water with its spines, which below were divided at the curved points, being like the horns of the moon, which are semicircular. And in such a shape are the ends of the tails of fish, semicircular.

b. κήτεος ἀλκαίη: the tail. Properly the lion's tail is called ἀλκαία, from the fact that through it the animal turns to strength. And the poet (Iliad 20.170): "with his tail he lashes his sides and flanks on both sides." But Callimachus has wrongly used it of mice (fr. 317 Schn.): "drawing from the tail." Or from ἀλαλκεῖν, that is, to help; just as οὐρά either from
οὐρεῖν, that is, to guard, or because animals stir themselves with their tail, as the lion, the bull, the dog, and the rest.

c. 〈ἀλκαίη:〉 properly the lion's tail is called ἀλκαία, the one that urges to strength. But in the Comic Lexicon (Didymus fr. I 5, 35 Schmidt 71) not only the lion's, but also the horse's, the ox's, and those of similar animals, as many as use the tail as a means of defense.
1619. ἥρωες, τέρας: he calls Triton a monster, since he has some parts of a man and some of a sea-monster.
1620. Ἀργῷός τε λιμήν: near Lake Tritonis there is a harbor called Argoos.
1630. αὔλιος: the evening star; either from αὐλίζεσθαι, that is, to sleep, or from spending time in the courtyards at that hour when the evening star rises.
1633. ἐπερρώοντο: they drove vigorously. Lᵐ P
1636. Κάρπαθος: it is an island of the Sporades near Cos. Homer has called it (Iliad 2.676) "Carpathos and Casos." But others call it Crapathos.
1638. 〈Τάλως:〉 proper name. Lᵍ
1640. ἐπιωγήν: shelter, by which the wind is broken. L Sᵐ (P)
1646-48. [τοὺς δὲ Τάλως] 〈ὑπαὶ δέ οἱ ἔσκε〉: Talos had on his ankle a tube enclosed in a membrane. It is called a tube
